title: The Sea-Wolf
description: Published in 1904 and the best of London's sea novels: a literary critic is rescued from a shipwreck by a seal-hunting schooner commanded by a Nietzschean brute.
plot_or_argument: Humphrey Van Weyden, a soft civilised critic, is taken aboard the Ghost by Captain Wolf Larsen, who rules his crew by force and philosophy; Humphrey is toughened by the ship, falls in love with the poet Maud Brewster, and escapes with her to an island where he finally defeats the dying Larsen.
principal_characters: Wolf Larsen; Humphrey Van Weyden; Maud Brewster; Mugridge; Johansen; Louis; Death Larsen
historical_context: 1904: the American seal-hunting fleet of the Pacific, the vogue of Nietzsche in America, and the debate on individualism and the 'superman'.
literary_significance: The Sea-Wolf is London's most intellectually ambitious novel and the central American fictional treatment of Nietzsche: Larsen is one of the great American characters, and the novel's conflict between the superman's philosophy and the civilised values of Humphrey and Maud is the most direct American response to Nietzsche's ideas in the period.

title: Martin Eden
description: Published in 1909 and London's most personal novel: the self-education of a sailor into a writer, and his destruction by the success he achieves.
plot_or_argument: Martin Eden, a rough sailor, educates himself to win the hand of Ruth Morse, a bourgeois girl; he reads Spencer and Swinburne, writes stories that nobody will buy, is rejected by Ruth's family, and then becomes famous overnight, after which he discovers that success means nothing and that the woman he loved cannot understand him.
principal_characters: Martin Eden; Ruth Morse; Lizzie Connolly; Joe Dawson; Brissenden; Mr Morse
historical_context: 1909: the American magazine market, the socialist movement of the 1900s, the intellectual self-education of the autodidact, and the American cult of success.
literary_significance: Martin Eden is London's masterpiece and one of the great American novels about the writer's life: its account of the market for fiction, its critique of the American success ideal and its autobiographical ending made it the most searching American novel of the artist between James and Fitzgerald.

title: The Iron Heel
description: Published in 1908 and the first modern American dystopia: the rise of a fascist oligarchy in the United States and the crushing of the working class.
plot_or_argument: A manuscript of the 1930s, annotated by a scholar of a later socialist era, records the rise of the Iron Heel, the American oligarchy that destroys the socialist movement after 1912, the failed Chicago Commune and the extermination of the revolutionaries, and the long dark age that follows before the final triumph of the brotherhood of man.
principal_characters: Ernest Everhard; Avis Everhard; Bishop; Wickson; Pendar; the Iron Heel
historical_context: 1908: the American labour wars of the 1900s, the socialist movement of Eugene Debs, the Russian revolution of 1905, and the fear of monopoly capital.
literary_significance: The Iron Heel is the first modern American dystopia and the founding text of the American political novel of the future: it anticipates Orwell, Huxley and Zamiatin, it invented the fictional future history annotated from a later age, and it is the most radical American novel of the period.

title: 'To Build a Fire'
description: Published in 1908 in the revised version and the greatest American story of the wilderness: a man freezes to death in the Yukon because he has built his fire in the wrong place.
plot_or_argument: A cheechako travels alone through the Yukon at seventy-five below zero, against the advice of an old-timer; he breaks through the ice, soaks his feet, builds a fire under a spruce tree, and the snow from the tree falls and extinguishes it, after which he cannot light another, and the story ends with the dog watching him die.
historical_context: 1902-08: the Klondike trail, the science of hypothermia, the American naturalist view of nature as indifferent, and the fashion for the survival story.
literary_significance: 'To Build a Fire' is the purest American naturalist story and one of the most perfect short stories in English: its reduction of a human life to the failure of a single fire is the naturalist thesis in narrative form, and it is the most anthologised American wilderness story ever written.

title: The House of Mirth
description: Published in 1905 and the novel that made Wharton famous: the destruction of a beautiful woman who cannot bring herself to sell herself in the marriage market.
plot_or_argument: Lily Bart, a beautiful but poor member of old New York society, is caught between the need for a rich husband and her refusal to marry a man she does not love; a series of social mishaps and her own fatal indecision strip her of her position, her friends and her last chances, and she dies alone in a shabby boarding-house, having taken an overdose of sleeping medicine.
principal_characters: Lily Bart; Lawrence Selden; Simon Rosedale; Gus Trenor; Judy Trenor; Bertha Dorset; Gerty Farish; Mrs Peniston
historical_context: 1905: the New York of the Knickerbocker aristocracy, the 'dollar princess' marriages to European titles, the new rich of the Gilded Age, and the American debate on women's work.
literary_significance: The House of Mirth is the central American novel of the marriage market and the first great American novel of a woman's social destruction: its portrait of Lily Bart is one of the great American characters, and its analysis of the economics of marriage made it the founding text of the American novel of manners.

title: Ethan Frome
description: Published in 1911 and the most concentrated American tragedy of the period: three people trapped in a New England farmhouse and a hopeless love.
plot_or_argument: Ethan Frome, a poor farmer in the hill town of Starkfield, Massachusetts, is married to the sickly and tyrannical Zeena and in love with her young cousin Mattie; when Zeena determines to send Mattie away, Ethan and Mattie attempt a double suicide by sledding into a tree, and the novel ends years later with both crippled and living in the Frome house under Zeena's care.
principal_characters: Ethan Frome; Zeena Frome; Mattie Silver; the narrator; Harmon Gow; Mrs Hale
historical_context: 1911: the declining hill farms of western Massachusetts, the New England winter, the rural poor, and the American regionalist tradition of Jewett and Freeman.
literary_significance: Ethan Frome is the most perfect short novel in American literature and Wharton's masterpiece of tragic inevitability: its use of the New England landscape, its framing narrator and its terrible ending make it a classic, and it is the finest American example of the regional tragedy.

title: The Custom of the Country
description: Published in 1913 and the most satirical of Wharton's novels: the rise of a beautiful, ruthless midwestern girl through three marriages.
plot_or_argument: Undine Spragg, a beautiful girl from Apex City, comes to New York determined to have everything; she marries Ralph Marvell for his name, leaves him for a French nobleman, divorces him for a richer man, and finally, with her son lost to her, achieves the marriage she has wanted, only to find that there is nothing left she wants.
principal_characters: Undine Spragg; Ralph Marvell; Elmer Moffatt; Raymond de Chelles; Peter Van Degen; Clare Van Degen; Paul Marvell
historical_context: 1913: the new rich of the Gilded Age, the American divorce colony in Paris, the 'dollar princess' marriages, and the emergence of the culture of celebrity.
literary_significance: The Custom of the Country is the greatest American satire of the period and the finest novel of American social climbing: its portrait of Undine Spragg is one of the most complete characters in American fiction, and its analysis of the relation between money, marriage and nationality makes it the central American novel of the new rich.

title: The Age of Innocence
description: Published in 1920 and the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel of old New York: a man's love for a woman the society of the 1870s cannot accept.
plot_or_argument: Newland Archer, a young lawyer of old New York, is engaged to May Welland when her cousin the Countess Ellen Olenska returns from Europe, separated from her Polish husband; Newland falls in love with Ellen, and the novel follows his renunciation, his marriage to May and his long life afterwards, ending with his refusal to see Ellen again in Paris.
principal_characters: Newland Archer; May Welland; Ellen Olenska; Mrs Manson Mingott; Julius Beaufort; Sillerton Jackson; Lawrence Lefferts
historical_context: 1920: the New York of the 1870s, the codes of the Knickerbocker aristocracy, the First World War and the vanished world it destroyed.
literary_significance: The Age of Innocence is Wharton's masterpiece and the greatest American novel of manners: it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921, it is the definitive portrait of old New York, and its analysis of the cost of social conformity made it one of the central American novels of the twentieth century.

title: Tales of Men and Ghosts
description: Published in 1910 and the best of Wharton's supernatural collections: ten stories of the uncanny set in the drawing rooms of the New York and European upper class.
plot_or_argument: The ghost stories — 'Afterward', 'The Eyes', 'The Triumph of Night', 'Kerfol' — present hauntings that are always also moral facts: a house that is haunted by a crime, a pair of eyes at a window, a young man's spectral companion who is Death, and a castle whose dogs remember a murdered woman.
historical_context: 1898-1910: the American vogue for the ghost story after James and Bierce, the country houses of New England and Europe, and the new psychology of the unconscious.
literary_significance: Tales of Men and Ghosts contains the finest American ghost stories after Henry James: 'Afterward' and 'The Eyes' are permanent classics of the form, and Wharton's treatment of the supernatural as a moral and psychological fact rather than a sensation made her the most sophisticated American writer of ghost stories in the period.

title: Tales of Soldiers and Civilians
description: Published in 1891 and the greatest American collection of Civil War stories: the war as a series of private encounters with death and illusion.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge', in which a planter is hanged and his escape occurs only in the instant before death, 'Chickamauga', in which a deaf child wanders through a battlefield, and 'A Horseman in the Sky', in which a sentry shoots his own father, among other stories of soldiers and civilians caught by the war.
historical_context: 1861-65 and 1891: the Civil War, the American cult of the veteran, the new magazine fiction of the 1880s, and the American reception of Poe.
literary_significance: Tales of Soldiers and Civilians is the greatest American book about the Civil War after Crane: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' invented the modern ironic short story, and Bierce's cold technique — the delayed revelation, the reversed ending — made the collection a founding text of the modern American short story.

title: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge'
description: Published in 1890 and the most famous American short story of the nineteenth century: a Confederate planter's escape from execution exists only in the final moment of his life.
plot_or_argument: Peyton Farquhar stands on a bridge over Owl Creek with a rope round his neck; the rope breaks, he falls into the water, escapes the bullets, swims downstream, and walks all night to his home and his wife — and then the story returns to the bridge, where his body hangs, and the escape is revealed as the last thought of a dying man.
historical_context: 1862 and 1890: the Union occupation of northern Alabama, the laws of war, the American cult of the planter-hero, and the 1890s vogue for the trick story.
literary_significance: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' is the most anthologised American short story of the century and one of the foundations of the modern short story: its manipulation of time and its revelation of the escape as a dying illusion influenced writers from O. Henry to Borges, and it remains the model of the ironic American story.

title: The Devil's Dictionary
description: Published as The Cynic's Word Book in 1906 and as The Devil's Dictionary in 1911: the great American work of satire, in the form of a dictionary of cynical definitions.
plot_or_argument: The book defines the vocabulary of American public life — politics, religion, law, journalism, marriage, money — in a series of epigrams that reverse the official meanings, so that a 'painting' becomes a way of protecting flat surfaces from the weather and exposing them to the critic.
historical_context: 1881-1911: the American newspaper culture of the Gilded Age, the Hearst press, the satirical tradition of Swift and Voltaire, and the American disbelief of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Devil's Dictionary is the great American work of satire and one of the most quoted books in American literature: it is the source of a large part of the American vocabulary of cynicism, and its definitions of politics, religion and the press remain the permanent American critique of official language.

title: Can Such Things Be?
description: Published in 1893 and the best American collection of supernatural tales of the century: twenty-four stories of ghosts, revenants and inexplicable events.
plot_or_argument: The stories include 'The Damned Thing', in which an invisible creature kills a man in the California hills, 'The Death of Halpin Frayser', in which a man is murdered by his mother's corpse, and 'The Moonlit Road', in which a murder is narrated three times from three points of view.
historical_context: 1889-93: the American vogue for the supernatural after Poe, the new psychology of the Society for Psychical Research, and the Californian frontier setting.
literary_significance: Can Such Things Be? is the finest American supernatural collection of the period and the central book of American weird fiction before Lovecraft: its invisible monster, its corpse-bride and its multiple narration made it a founding text of the American weird tale, and Lovecraft named Bierce as one of his masters.

title: Fantastic Fables
description: Published in 1899 and Bierce's American version of Aesop: short, savage political fables about politicians, journalists and the human animal.
plot_or_argument: The fables take the form of the classical apologue but turn it into political satire: a statesman is shown to be a thief, a journalist to be a liar, a reformer to be a fool, and the moral is invariably the opposite of the official one.
historical_context: 1899: the American politics of the Gilded Age, the Spanish-American War and the imperial debate, the Hearst press, and the tradition of the political fable from Swift to Twain.
literary_significance: Fantastic Fables is the most concentrated American political satire of the period and the best American imitation of Aesop: its savage reduction of public life to animal behaviour made it a permanent text of American political cynicism, and it is the model for the modern American political fable.

title: Main-Travelled Roads
description: Published in 1891 and the founding American book of the farm: six stories of the drudgery, debt and loneliness of the Middle Border.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow the farmers of Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota: the daughter who returns from the city to find her mother worn out by labour, the man who has lost his farm to the mortgage, the hired girl who is seduced and abandoned, and the brothers who meet again after years of resentment — each shown without romance and without pity.
historical_context: 1887-91: the agricultural depression of the 1880s, the Populist movement, the single-tax agitation of Henry George, and the American revolt against the rural idyll.
literary_significance: Main-Travelled Roads is the founding text of American agrarian realism and the central literary document of the Populist movement: its portraits of the farm wife and the mortgaged farmer destroyed the sentimental picture of American rural life and made Garland the most influential American short-story writer of the 1890s after Crane.

title: Rose of Dutcher's Coolly
description: Published in 1895 and the first American novel of the farm girl who escapes to the city: the education and emancipation of a Wisconsin farmer's daughter.
plot_or_argument: Rose Dutcher grows up in the Wisconsin countryside, loses her mother, is sent to the state university by her father, and becomes a writer in Chicago; she refuses the marriage her father expects, takes a lover, and insists on her right to live as an artist and a free woman.
historical_context: 1895: the Wisconsin farm of the 1880s, the state university and the Chicago of the World's Fair, and the American debate on the New Woman.
literary_significance: Rose of Dutcher's Coolly is the first American novel of the farm girl's escape and one of the earliest American feminist novels: its refusal of the marriage plot and its insistence on a woman's right to work and to sexual freedom made it a landmark of the American New Woman novel.

title: Crumbling Idols
description: Published in 1894 and the manifesto of American 'veritism': twelve essays calling for an American literature grounded in the actual life of the American West.
plot_or_argument: Garland argues that American literature must abandon European models and the genteel tradition, that the West and the Middle Border are the true American subject, that local colour is the foundation of national literature, and that the artist must record the actual conditions of life rather than the ideal.
historical_context: 1894: the American copyright debate, the genteel tradition of the eastern magazines, the Populist movement, and the Chicago of the World's Columbian Exposition.
literary_significance: Crumbling Idols is the founding manifesto of American literary nationalism after Whitman: its doctrine of 'veritism' gave the American realists their theory, its call for a western literature anticipated the Chicago Renaissance, and it is the central American critical text of the 1890s.

title: A Son of the Middle Border
description: Published in 1917 and the Pulitzer Prize-winning memoir of the American frontier: Garland's own childhood on the moving edge of settlement.
plot_or_argument: Garland remembers his Wisconsin boyhood, the family's removal to Iowa and then to Dakota, the labour of the homestead, his mother's exhaustion and his father's disappointed hopes, and his own escape to Boston, in a narrative that records the closing of the frontier as a family experience.
historical_context: 1850s-90s and 1917: the westward movement, the Homestead Act, the depression of 1893, and the American retrospect on the frontier after Turner.
literary_significance: A Son of the Middle Border is one of the great American autobiographies and the definitive personal record of the westward movement: it won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography in 1922, it is the source of much of the American memory of the frontier, and it stands with Garland's stories as the central literary document of the Middle Border.

title: Old Creole Days
description: Published in 1879 and the founding American book of New Orleans: eight stories of Creole life in the old French quarter.
plot_or_argument: The stories present the courtyards and the codes of the old Creole families — the ruined aristocrat, the quadroon woman, the young man who marries beneath him, the usurer and the orphan — in a series of gentle, exact narratives that end in renunciation or in a quiet disappointment.
historical_context: 1873-79: the post-war New Orleans, the decline of the Creole aristocracy, the mixed-race society of the French quarter, and the American local-colour movement.
literary_significance: Old Creole Days created the literary image of New Orleans: it was the first American book to record the speech, architecture and manners of French Louisiana, it founded the southern local-colour school, and it remains the source of the American idea of the Creole city.

title: The Grandissimes: A Story of Creole Life
description: Published in 1880 and the first great American novel of New Orleans: the feud of two Creole families in the years after the Louisiana Purchase.
plot_or_argument: Honoré Grandissime, a young Creole, returns to New Orleans in 1803 and is drawn into the feud between his family and the Fusiliers; he loves Aurora Nancanou, whose family his has ruined, and his half-brother, the free man of colour also called Honoré Grandissime, becomes the novel's moral centre, in a story that ends with renunciation and a divided inheritance.
principal_characters: Honoré Grandissime; Honoré Grandissime (f.m.c.); Aurora Nancanou; Clotilde; Dr Keene; Agricola Fusilier; Palmyre Philosophe
historical_context: 1803-04 and 1880: the Louisiana Purchase, the free people of colour of New Orleans, the Code Noir, and the racial order of the post-Reconstruction South.
literary_significance: The Grandissimes is the first great American novel of the deep South and the most important American novel about race before Twain: its treatment of the free man of colour, its portrait of a society built on racial hierarchy and its refusal of a sentimental resolution make it a central text of the American literature of race.

title: Madame Delphine
description: Published in 1881 and Cable's most concentrated story of race and love in old New Orleans: a quadroon woman's sacrifice for her daughter's future.
plot_or_argument: Madame Delphine, a free woman of colour who has kept her past secret, discovers that her daughter Olive is loved by a young white Creole; knowing that the match is impossible unless her own history is hidden, she arranges the marriage and then takes her own life rather than reveal the truth.
historical_context: 1881: the racial codes of New Orleans, the position of the free people of colour, and the American debate on interracial marriage.
literary_significance: Madame Delphine is the most concentrated American story of the colour line before Chesnutt: its portrait of a mother's sacrifice and its unflinching analysis of the racial law made it one of the most discussed American stories of 1881 and it remains a central text of the American literature of race.

title: The Silent South
description: Published in 1885 and the most courageous white southern book of the century on race: essays demanding civil rights and an end to the convict-lease system.
plot_or_argument: Cable argues that the South must accept the black citizen as an equal before the law, attacks the convict-lease system as slavery under another name, defends the public school for both races, and calls on the southern churches to lead the work of reconciliation.
historical_context: 1885: the end of Reconstruction, the convict-lease system, the rise of Jim Crow, the Plessy case a decade later, and the northern review culture of the 1880s.
literary_significance: The Silent South is the central white southern text of the American struggle for racial justice in the nineteenth century: it cost Cable his southern audience and his livelihood, it was answered by every defender of the New South, and it remains one of the most important American documents of the post-Reconstruction debate on race.

title: A New England Nun and Other Stories
description: Published in 1891 and the finest American collection of New England village stories: the small, exact lives of unmarried and widowed women.
plot_or_argument: The title story follows Louisa Ellis, who has waited fourteen years to marry Joe Dagget and realises, when he returns, that she prefers her quiet house and her little dog; the other stories present the village widow, the woman who keeps house for a man who does not notice her, and the girl who is left behind, each settled in a single afternoon.
historical_context: 1887-91: the declining rural villages of Massachusetts and Vermont, the surplus of unmarried women in New England, and the local-colour movement after Jewett.
literary_significance: A New England Nun is the central American book of the unmarried woman and one of the finest story collections of the nineteenth century: its title story is a permanent classic, and Freeman's exact, unsentimental portraits of village women made her the most important American regionalist after Jewett and a founding figure for the feminist criticism of American literature.

title: A Humble Romance and Other Stories
description: Published in 1887 and Freeman's first collection: twenty-eight stories of the poor and the obscure in the New England villages.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow the pedlars, the hired girls, the poor relations and the old women of the Massachusetts hill towns through courtships, deaths and disappointments, each rendered in the plain speech of the village and each ending with a small, unremarked tragedy or a moment of unexpected dignity.
historical_context: 1884-87: the rural poverty of post-war New England, the decline of the hill farms, and the American local-colour market of Harper's and the Century.
literary_significance: A Humble Romance established Freeman as the finest American writer of the village poor and made her reputation as a regionalist: its stories of hired girls and pedlars are among the earliest American fictions of working-class women, and it prepared the way for the masterpiece of 1891.

title: Pembroke: A Novel
description: Published in 1894 and Freeman's finest novel: two New England families divided by pride and a broken engagement.
plot_or_argument: Barnabas Thayer breaks his engagement to Charlotte Barnard because of wounded pride, and the two families — the Thayers and the Barnards — are set against one another for years; the novel follows Charlotte's long fidelity, Barnabas's decline into drink and illness, and the slow reconciliation that comes only at the end.
historical_context: 1894: the Massachusetts village of the 1890s, the stern Congregational culture of the New England interior, and the American regional novel of the 1890s.
literary_significance: Pembroke is Freeman's masterpiece and one of the finest American regional novels of the century: its portrait of a community governed by pride and its study of a woman's long patience made it the fullest expression of her vision, and it is the equal of Jewett's best work.
